561.event_title: John Adams defends the British soldiers after the Boston Massacre
561.place: Boston, Massachusetts (then a British colony), United States
561.event: After British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston on 5 March 1770, Captain Thomas Preston and eight soldiers were indicted, and John Adams agreed to serve on their unpopular defence team. Preston was acquitted on 30 October 1770 after a trial lasting longer than a day, and in the soldiers' trial, decided on 5 December 1770, six men were acquitted and two were found guilty of manslaughter rather than murder. The two convicted men avoided the death penalty by pleading benefit of clergy and were branded on the hand instead.
561.explanation: In a town furious at the army, the case was settled by testimony heard in court, and the verdicts distinguished between the men according to what each had actually done.
561.tie_back: The kural says a true ruler first inquires impartially and then punishes in measure with the offence, and the Boston trials show inquiry before judgement and a penalty matched to the proven wrong rather than to public anger.
561._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of impartial inquiry followed by proportionate punishment, though it is a colonial court rather than a king acting personally.

562.event_title: The Meiji government pardons the rebel admiral Enomoto Takeaki
562.event: Enomoto Takeaki, who had led the last forces loyal to the former shogunate, surrendered to the new Meiji government at the fortress of Goryokaku in Hakodate in June 1869. He was sent to Tokyo and held in confinement for about three years, after which he was pardoned. He went on to serve the government as envoy to Russia and held several ministerial posts.
562.explanation: The new government crushed the armed rebellion completely, but the penalty that followed was limited, and the former rebel became one of its useful servants.
562.tie_back: The kural advises raising the rod sternly but letting it fall gently, and Enomoto's defeat, brief confinement and pardon show severity in the contest and mildness in the punishment.
562._accuracy_note: A good fit for stern action followed by mild punishment; the kural's promise of lasting prosperity is suggested by the Meiji state's later success but cannot be traced to this one decision.

563.event_title: The harsh Qin dynasty collapses soon after the First Emperor's death
563.event: The state of Qin unified China in 221 BCE, and its ruler, known as Qin Shi Huang, governed through a rigid Legalist legal system with severe punishments, heavy taxation and forced labour on great building projects. After his death in 210 BCE, revolts and fighting broke out across the empire. The dynasty collapsed by 207-206 BCE, less than four years after his death, and was soon replaced by the Han dynasty.
563.explanation: The first dynasty to unite all China, ruling largely through fear of punishment, lasted only about fifteen years, one of the shortest-lived major dynasties in Chinese history.
563.tie_back: The kural predicts that a cruel-sceptred ruler who habitually fills his people with dread will certainly and swiftly be ruined, and the Qin dynasty fell almost as soon as its founder was gone.
563._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's claim of certain and swift ruin for rule by dread, with the caveat that succession struggles at court also contributed to the fall.

564.event_title: Nicolae Ceausescu is shouted down at his last rally
564.event: On 21 December 1989 Romania's ruler Nicolae Ceausescu addressed a large organised rally in Bucharest, broadcast live, to condemn the unrest in Timisoara. Partway through the speech people in the crowd began shouting against him, the broadcast was briefly cut, and he was unable to continue. The next day he and his wife fled the capital by helicopter, were taken into custody by the army, and on 25 December were tried by a special military tribunal and executed.
564.explanation: Within four days of the moment the crowd openly voiced its verdict on him, a ruler who had held power for nearly a quarter of a century had lost everything.
564.tie_back: The kural says a king whom the people call cruel will have his span cut short and perish quickly, and the shouting at Ceausescu's rally was followed in days by the end of his rule and his life.
564._accuracy_note: A very close fit to the kural's picture of the people's bitter word followed by the ruler's swift end; the event field is kept factual and brief because of its violent conclusion.

565.event_title: Emperor Rudolf II withdraws into Prague Castle with his collections
565.event: Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II moved his court to Prague in 1583, and in later years, subject to severe depression, he lived in seclusion there among his vast collections of art, curiosities and scientific instruments. The Habsburg archdukes, dissatisfied with his government, forced him in 1608 to give up Hungary, Austria and Moravia to his brother Matthias. In 1611 Matthias's army virtually held him prisoner in Prague until he yielded Bohemia as well, and he died there in January 1612.
565.explanation: Rudolf owned one of the greatest treasure collections in Europe, yet as he grew more withdrawn and hard to reach, his family and subjects turned to his brother and his power slipped away.
565.tie_back: The kural likens the wealth of a ruler who is hard to see to treasure held by a demon, and Rudolf's famous collections, locked away with a secluded emperor, did nothing to keep his crowns.
565._accuracy_note: Fits the kural's point about an inaccessible ruler and useless wealth, but the sources stress his illness and political incompetence rather than a scowling or harsh manner.

566.event_title: Sultan Osman II's harsh measures against the Janissaries end his reign
566.event: After the Ottoman army's failure at Khotin in 1621, the young Sultan Osman II blamed the Janissary corps, cut their pay and closed their coffee shops, and planned to raise a new army to break their power. Hearing of his plans and already resentful of his treatment, the Janissaries revolted in May 1622. They deposed him on 19 May and killed him the following day, restoring his uncle Mustafa I to the throne.
566.explanation: Osman's reign of about four years ended almost at once when the soldiers he had treated with open contempt turned against him.
566.tie_back: The kural warns that a ruler harsh in speech and lacking kindly regard loses even great wealth on the spot, and Osman's treatment of his own troops cost him his throne in a matter of days.
566._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows a ruler's lack of regard for those around him producing sudden ruin, but the sources document harsh measures rather than harsh words, and the Janissaries' own grievances were also at work.

567.event: Between the 1690s and about 1750 Parliament passed many laws making specified crimes, including some thefts of small value, punishable by death, a body of law later known as the Bloody Code. In 1832 opponents of capital punishment argued in Parliament that such severity discouraged victims from prosecuting and juries from convicting, though others disputed this. Robert Peel, as Home Secretary from 1822, carried a broad consolidation and reform of the criminal law between 1825 and 1830, and most of the capital statutes were repealed in the 1820s and 1830s.
567.explanation: Punishments far beyond the measure of the offence did not strengthen the law; reformers argued that they weakened it, and Parliament eventually abandoned them.
567.tie_back: The kural calls punishment beyond measure a file that slowly wears away a ruler's strength, and the Bloody Code's long, gradual discrediting shows excess eroding rather than reinforcing authority.
567._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of excessive punishment undermining the power it was meant to serve, though the kural speaks of a king's strength against enemies and historians still debate how far juries resisted the code.

568.event_title: Ibrahim Lodi alienates his nobles and loses the Delhi Sultanate
568.event: Ibrahim Lodi, sultan of Delhi from 1517, tried to rule more autocratically than his father and became increasingly suspicious and harsh toward his Afghan nobles, some of whom rebelled. Resenting his attempts to curb their authority, Dawlat Khan Lodi, governor of the Punjab, and Alam Khan Lodi, Ibrahim's uncle, appealed to Babur, the ruler of Kabul, for help. Babur invaded, and Ibrahim was defeated and killed at the First Battle of Panipat in April 1526, ending the Lodi dynasty.
568.explanation: A sultan who ruled without carrying his nobles with him and treated them with suspicion and harshness found his own governors inviting a foreign enemy against him.
568.tie_back: The kural says a king who does not deliberate with his circle and then flares at them in anger will see his fortune shrink, and Ibrahim's quarrels with his nobles led directly to the loss of his kingdom.
568._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a ruler alienating his own court and losing his fortune; the sources stress his autocracy and harshness more than a specific failure to take counsel.

569.event_title: France enters the Franco-German War unprepared and the Second Empire falls
569.event: France declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870, but its armies were slow to mobilise and not ready to fight when German forces crossed the border, with shortages of equipment reported among the units. One French army was soon bottled up in Metz, and on 1-2 September at Sedan, Emperor Napoleon III was captured and a French army of nearly 100,000 men surrendered. On 4 September, after news of the defeat reached Paris, the Second Empire was overthrown and a republic was proclaimed.
569.explanation: An empire that went to war without having readied its defences collapsed within about six weeks of the first battles.
569.tie_back: The kural warns that a ruler who has not prepared his defences beforehand will be seized with fear when war comes and quickly perish, and Napoleon III's unready empire fell almost as soon as the fighting began.
569._accuracy_note: A strong fit for swift ruin through lack of preparation; the chapter's link between unpreparedness and earlier rule by dread is not part of this example.

570.event: In 1565 Tsar Ivan IV set aside a large part of his realm as the oprichnina, a territory under his direct personal control, and formed a personal force, the oprichniki, which grew to several thousand men. Through them he carried out years of terror against boyars, towns and ordinary people, including the devastation of Novgorod in 1570. When the oprichniki failed to defend Moscow against a Crimean Tatar attack in 1571, Ivan abolished the oprichnina in 1572.
570.explanation: A ruler who governed by terror bound to himself a body of men whose only qualification was loyalty to his will, and they inflicted lasting damage on the country while failing it in a real emergency.
570.tie_back: The kural calls a harsh sceptre that gathers unworthy helpers the heaviest burden the earth can bear, and the oprichnina shows how such a ruler and his chosen enforcers together weighed upon an entire land.
570._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of tyranny exercised through a body of chosen enforcers; the kural's specific stress on their lack of learning is not documented for the oprichniki.
